name: Sildenafil

card.summary: A PDE5-inhibitor tablet (Viagra) that widens blood vessels, which some lifters use hoping for fuller-looking muscle pumps and better circulation.
card.note: Prescription drug in most countries; must not be combined with nitrate medicines. Appearance uses are community claims rather than approved indications.

quick.overview:
Sildenafil is the active ingredient in Viagra. It is approved for erectile dysfunction and for pulmonary arterial hypertension. It works by blocking the enzyme PDE5, which relaxes smooth muscle and widens blood vessels.

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is discussed for its vasodilating effect: the hope is better blood flow to muscle (fuller pumps, vascularity) and, in some threads, better sexual confidence and function. Published trials cover erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; the muscle-and-hair claims made on forums have not been tested in the same way.
quick.how: Forum users describe taking it as an oral tablet, sometimes as a daily 'maintenance' drug, sometimes before training or sexual activity, and compare it with tadalafil (Cialis), which lasts longer. Some threads discuss combining PDE5 inhibitors with other hair or muscle protocols. Effects of the drug on erections are felt within an hour or so according to labelling.
quick.risks: Common effects are headache, flushing, indigestion, nasal congestion and visual changes such as a blue tint. Rare serious events include priapism, sudden vision or hearing loss and dangerously low blood pressure, and it is contraindicated with nitrate drugs. It is prescription-only in most countries, though the UK sells a 50 mg form (Viagra Connect) over the counter after a pharmacist consultation.

lead: Sildenafil, sold as Viagra (erectile dysfunction) and Revatio (pulmonary arterial hypertension), is a selective phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor developed by Pfizer. The US FDA approved it on 27 March 1998 as the first oral treatment for erectile dysfunction, and it has since become one of the best-known medicines in the world.[2][3]

Its appearance relevance comes from what it does to blood vessels. By blocking the breakdown of cGMP, it relaxes smooth muscle and widens vessels.[1][3] In looksmaxxing, bodybuilding and biohacking circles this is discussed in three ways: as a source of fuller muscle pumps and vascularity during training, as a way to restore or protect sexual function and the confidence that goes with it, and, in a few threads, as a milder-seeming alternative to steroids and SARMs for strength and muscle.[5][6][7] Posters also discuss it next to its longer-acting relative tadalafil (Cialis) and alongside hair-growth drugs such as oral minoxidil.[6][7]

The research record is large for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.[1][4][14] For muscle, a small 2013 randomised trial in 11 men reported higher muscle protein synthesis and less fatigue after eight days of low-dose sildenafil, while strength did not change.[9] Studies of blood flow in exercising muscle found an increase in older men but not in young men, and a study of forearm exercise in healthy young adults found no change in blood flow.[10][11][12] No trial has tested sildenafil for visible vascularity, hair or facial appearance in healthy people.

chain: Relaxes smooth muscle and widens blood vessels
Users hope for fuller pumps and vascularity while training, and for reliable sexual function and confidence
angle.text: Users who take it around training say they notice fuller-looking muscles and more vascularity, and some also value the confidence that comes with reliable sexual function. The vasodilation itself is the drug's documented mechanism; the cosmetic payoff is what forum users report, and controlled studies of exercising muscle in healthy young people have had mixed results.

paras: Sildenafil is approved for erectile dysfunction and, at a different dose form, for pulmonary arterial hypertension.[2][3] It is also used off label for secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, where reviews describe a moderate reduction in how often and how long vasospastic attacks last.[2] Researchers have examined it in many other settings, including neonatal pulmonary hypertension, where an open-label randomised trial of 36 newborns found that oral sildenafil lowered pulmonary pressure faster than bosentan.[15] A 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials in connective-tissue-disease pulmonary hypertension included sildenafil among the drugs that, as a group, improved functional class and six-minute walk distance versus placebo.[16]

Appearance interest centres on vasodilation. Forum posters describe taking it for training pumps, vascularity and sexual confidence, and some discuss it alongside hair-growth drugs.[5][6] One looksmax.org thread pitches it as a holistic option that avoids the hair loss, acne and blood-work burden its author associates with anabolic steroids.[5] Other threads compare Viagra with Cialis, with several posters saying they prefer Cialis for its longer duration and fewer side effects, and others asking how to obtain either drug without a prescription.[7][17]

Some posters describe the drug as a performance aid for sexual situations among young men without a diagnosed condition. A study summarised on Wikipedia found that a low dose did not change erection quality in men without erectile dysfunction but shortened the recovery time after ejaculation, with a strong placebo response.[2]

Nitric oxide released in the corpus cavernosum activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP, which relaxes smooth muscle and lets blood flow in. PDE5 normally breaks cGMP down; sildenafil, whose structure resembles cGMP, competes for the enzyme so that cGMP persists.[2][3] The drug does not cause arousal on its own and needs sexual stimulation to work for erectile dysfunction.[2][3] The same pathway operates in the lung vasculature, which is the basis of its use in pulmonary hypertension, and in other vascular smooth muscle, which explains side effects such as flushing and headache.[1][2]

Reference sources list oral bioavailability of about 41%, protein binding of about 96%, an onset of about 20 minutes, and a half-life of three to four hours. Metabolism is mainly by liver CYP3A4, with a minor role for CYP2C9, and most of a dose leaves in faeces. A high-fat meal slows absorption and lowers the peak level by nearly a third.[2] Its main metabolite, N-desmethylsildenafil, retains roughly 40-50% of the parent drug's PDE5 potency.[2]

Pfizer chemists led by Simon Campbell synthesised the compound, coded UK-92,480, in 1989 at the company's Sandwich, Kent, site while studying treatments for hypertension and angina.[2] Early trials, with the first clinical work at Morriston Hospital in Swansea, showed little effect on angina but frequent erections, and Pfizer redirected development to erectile dysfunction, a case often cited as drug repositioning.[2] The drug was patented in 1996 and approved by the FDA on 27 March 1998, going on sale in the US later that year.[2] The 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Furchgott, Murad and Ignarro for their work on nitric oxide signalling, the pathway the drug acts on.[2]

Viagra held about 92% of the global prescription erectile-dysfunction market in 2000, a share that fell to about 50% by 2007 as Cialis, Levitra, counterfeits and vision-loss reports took hold; annual Viagra sales peaked at about US$1.93 billion in 2008.[2] The Revatio patent expired in late 2012, with US generics from early 2013. Pfizer settled patent litigation with Teva and Mylan to allow US generics from December 2017, and the erectile-dysfunction patent expired in April 2020.[2] Canada's Supreme Court invalidated the Viagra patent on 8 November 2012, and EU patents lapsed in 2013.[2] Lower-priced generics widened access in many countries and are part of why the drug became familiar to online communities.[2]

sections.h: Research on healthy people, muscle and exercise
paras: Because looksmaxxing claims concern healthy users, studies of sildenafil in healthy volunteers are the closest research to those claims. They point in different directions depending on age, muscle group and outcome.

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2013 by Sheffield-Moore and colleagues at the University of Texas Medical Branch gave 25 mg of sildenafil or placebo daily for eight days to 11 generally healthy, mostly overweight men (five on sildenafil, six on placebo). Muscle-biopsy measurements showed higher muscle protein synthesis in the sildenafil group, which the authors described as roughly a doubling, and these men completed more repetitions in a fatiguing knee-extension test. Maximal isometric and isokinetic strength did not change. The authors noted the very small sample and short duration, and that effects on muscle mass and long-term use are unknown.[9] This is the study that forum posts cite when they describe the drug as boosting muscle protein synthesis.[5]

A 2015 study from the University of Copenhagen group (Nyberg and colleagues) compared 9 young men (average age 23) and 8 older men (average 72) on a control day and a day after sildenafil, during one-leg knee-extension exercise. In older men the drug raised leg blood flow, oxygen delivery (about 6-9%) and oxygen uptake (about 10-12%); young men showed no such changes. The authors suggested that reduced cGMP signalling may limit oxygen delivery to contracting muscle with ageing.[11]

A 2016 study at the Mayo Clinic (Limberg and colleagues) measured forearm blood flow by ultrasound during handgrip exercise in 30 healthy young adults. Sildenafil enhanced the vessels' response to a nitric oxide donor, so the drug was active, yet it did not change blood flow during the exercise; the authors concluded that nitric oxide and cGMP signalling play a minor role in exercise hyperaemia in healthy young people.[10] A companion analysis of the same group found no change in how fast blood vessels dilated at exercise onset with sildenafil alone.[12] Taken together, these reports describe measurable vascular effects without a consistent increase in muscle perfusion during exercise in healthy young adults, and no study has measured vein visibility or muscle fullness after training.
Other healthy-volunteer trials describe sympathetic nerve activation after sildenafil,[8] and changes in olfactory function.[18]

Common effects are headache, flushing, indigestion, nasal congestion and visual changes such as light sensitivity, blurred vision or a blue tint, the last attributed to weak activity against the PDE6 enzyme in the retina.[1][2] Rare serious events include priapism, severe low blood pressure, heart attack, ventricular arrhythmia, stroke, raised eye pressure and sudden hearing loss.[2] The FDA updated labelling in July 2005 after reports of sudden vision loss and in October 2007 added a more prominent hearing-loss warning to PDE5 inhibitors; a later pooled-data review found no evidence of increased risk of non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy.[2]

Nitrate medicines, nitric oxide donors such as nitroglycerin, and recreational alkyl nitrites ('poppers') are contraindicated because the combination can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure; riociguat is also contraindicated.[2] HIV protease inhibitors, erythromycin and cimetidine slow the drug's metabolism, and alpha-blockers can add to its blood-pressure lowering.[2] Labelling and clinicians advise against use when sexual activity is inadvisable for cardiovascular reasons.[2] Combining it with illicit drugs such as MDMA, stimulants or opioids has been reported among young recreational users.[2]

Sildenafil is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the EU and Australia (Schedule 4).[2] The UK trialled pharmacist-supervised sales at Boots in Manchester in 2007, and from early 2018 sold 50 mg Viagra Connect over the counter to adults after a pharmacist consultation. New Zealand allowed pharmacist sales from 2014, and Ireland, Poland, Norway and Portugal have introduced over-the-counter access as well.[2][3] Pfizer announced direct-to-consumer online sales in the US in May 2013, and many telehealth sites now prescribe after an online questionnaire.[2]

Counterfeit Viagra is among the world's most counterfeited medicines. A 2012 Pfizer study cited on Wikipedia found about 80% of sites claiming to sell Viagra were selling counterfeits, and fake tablets have been found to contain substances including amphetamine, metronidazole and boric acid.[2] Interpol reported in October 2023 that erectile-dysfunction medicines were the most seized category, at 22% of seizures.[2] Sildenafil analogues such as acetildenafil have also been found undeclared in 'herbal' sexual-enhancement supplements, and the FDA has banned or recalled such products.[2]

On looksmax.org, threads range from basic 'what does it do' questions to enthusiastic posts describing PDE5 inhibitors as broadly useful, with recurring questions about obtaining them without a prescription, comparisons of Viagra and Cialis, and questions about combining them with oral minoxidil.[5][6][7][17][19][20] Several replies in these threads are sceptical or joke about the claims.[5] Outside looksmaxxing, sildenafil is also a regular topic on Hacker News, where threads have discussed research on brain blood flow, Alzheimer's risk and its use as a cognitive 'smart drug'.[21][22] Some professional athletes have reportedly used it hoping for better muscle blood flow, according to media reports summarised on Wikipedia.[2]

Viagra was advertised directly to US consumers on television with endorsements from figures such as Bob Dole and Pelé.[2] The FDA objected in 2008 to a Viagra-branded online game that omitted risk information, and it was removed.[2]

Human trials examine erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; an early review describes improved erections across a range of causes.[1][4] Randomised trials have also tested sildenafil in neonatal pulmonary hypertension,[15] and pooled trials in connective-tissue-related pulmonary hypertension.[16] A 2021 Nature Aging study used network analysis of insurance-record data to identify sildenafil as a candidate drug for Alzheimer's disease, with randomised trials still needed to test the idea.[23] Healthy-volunteer studies of muscle protein synthesis, fatigue and exercise blood flow are described above.[9][10][11][12] Experimental work has also examined cGMP signalling in migraine induction.[24] No published trial has tested sildenafil for visible vascularity, muscle size gain over months, or hair appearance in healthy people.

FDA approves Viagra for erectile dysfunction on 27 March; the Nobel Prize goes to the nitric oxide signalling researchers.[2]
FDA updates PDE5 inhibitor labelling after reports of sudden vision loss.[2]

Revatio patent expires; Canada's Supreme Court invalidates the Viagra patent in November.[2]
US generics for Revatio begin; Sheffield-Moore trial reports higher muscle protein synthesis in eight-day sildenafil use.[2][9]
Generic Viagra becomes available in the US from December.[2]

US Viagra patent for erectile dysfunction expires in April.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sildenafil and tadalafil are discussed as circulation and confidence aids, often compared with each other and with steroids; some posts are earnest and others humorous.[5][7][19]

claims.claim: Viagra is a safer 'alternative to steroids and SARMs' for muscle
claims.believers: One poster argues it offers benefits without hair loss, acne or the need for cycling or bloodwork, calling it one of the most 'legit' substances available and citing a study on muscle protein synthesis.[5]
claims.experts: The cited trial enrolled 11 men for eight days, reported higher protein synthesis and less fatigue, and found no change in maximal strength; its authors note effects on muscle mass are unknown.[9] No trial has measured muscle gain over months in healthy users.

claims.claim: PDE5 inhibitors improve pumps and vascularity during training
claims.believers: Users describe fuller-looking muscles from the vessel-widening effect.[5]
claims.experts: Vasodilation is the drug's documented mechanism.[1][3] Studies in healthy young people found no change in forearm blood flow during exercise, while older men showed higher leg blood flow and oxygen delivery; visible vascularity has not been studied.[10][11]

claims.claim: Tadalafil is better than sildenafil for everyday use
claims.believers: Posters say Cialis lasts longer and gives them fewer side effects such as flushing and headache, and that combining PDE5 inhibitors is stronger.[7]
claims.experts: Sildenafil has a half-life of three to four hours and a labelled list of common side effects including flushing and headache.[2] Combining PDE5 inhibitors has not been studied for appearance goals.

claims.claim: It can be combined with oral minoxidil for hair
claims.believers: Posters ask whether pairing a vasodilating PDE5 inhibitor with oral minoxidil is useful or safe for hair and general circulation.[6]
claims.experts: Both drugs lower blood pressure, and sildenafil labelling cautions about additive blood-pressure lowering with other vasodilating drugs.[2] No published trial has tested the pairing for hair.

claims.claim: Taking it without a prescription is low-risk
claims.believers: Posters note the drug is widely used and sold over the counter in some countries.[5][19]
claims.experts: Labelling and reviews list headache, flushing and visual changes, rare serious cardiovascular events, and a contraindication with nitrates.[2] Counterfeit tablets are widespread in online sales.[2]

claims.claim: Young men without erectile problems gain performance or confidence from it
claims.believers: Users describe a confidence and performance boost, and some posters joke about accidental use.[7]
claims.experts: A study summarised on Wikipedia found no change in erection quality at a low dose in men without erectile dysfunction, with a strong placebo effect, though recovery time after ejaculation shortened.[2]

claims.claim: Viagra could protect the brain and heart
claims.believers: Hacker News commenters and forum posters point to headlines on brain blood flow and Alzheimer's risk.[21][22]
claims.experts: A 2021 Nature Aging analysis proposed sildenafil as a candidate drug for Alzheimer's disease and called for randomised trials; the findings come from computational and observational data.[23]
